Euler Collinearity

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Three lines drawn from a triangle's corners keep meeting at one point as you slide a number up or down; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the round points to move the triangle or the point P, then slide the number. Tick Show hint or Show names to see more, and press Reset to start over.
Look for the math

Move the triangle or the point P and the three lines still cross at a single spot. That spot travels along a straight line. The applet illustrates a generalization of a problem from the Mathematics Magazine; its own page explains that choosing P at the triangle's circumcenter gives the famous Euler line. The live page no longer embeds the Java applet, but the archived cut-the-knot page from 2011 does, and its <APPLET CODE="EulerCollinearity"> tag is the source for this port.

Shrinking the triangle around its center

Join the three side midpoints and you get a smaller upside-down triangle. It is the original triangle scaled by -1/2 about its centroid G. The slider applies a second scaling, by t about P, to each midpoint Mk, giving Mtk = P + t(Mk - P). Tick Show hint to see the two scaled midpoint triangles.

Where the three lines meet

Two scalings applied one after the other make another scaling. Its center lies on the line GP, and it carries each corner Vk to Mtk, so the three lines Vk Mtk all pass through that center. Its position is S(t) = (2(1-t)P + 3tG)/(2+t). At t = 0 it is P; at t = 1 it is G. The logic test checked this formula against the applet's own method of intersecting the lines for thousands of triangles, points and slider values. The page says "for any t"; that is true for the applet's slider, from -1 to 50.5, but at t = -2 the two scalings become a slide and the three lines are parallel instead of concurrent. The applet also stops drawing an intersection when two lines are less than one pixel from parallel, and this port keeps that quirk.

Why the Euler line turns up

If P is the circumcenter O, the line GP is the line through the circumcenter and centroid, which is the Euler line. As t grows, S approaches 3G - 2O, the orthocenter H, and GH = 2GO on that line. This differs from the separate Euler Line Simple applet: that one proves O, G and H lie on one line using parallelograms and altitudes, while this one studies how the meeting point moves when a point P and a slider change.

Put P on the circumcenter and slide t from 0 upwards: the green point travels from the circumcenter through the centroid towards the orthocenter.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
